hints: Focus on which halogen is more reactive and can displace the other from its salt solution.
Chlorine oxidises iodide ions to form iodine, so think about what colour iodine gives in aqueous solution.
Remember iodine dissolves much better in an organic solvent like hexane than in water, giving a vivid violet colour there.
walkthrough:
**Spot the displacement reaction**

Chlorine is above iodine in Group 17, so it is the stronger oxidising agent. It will displace iodine from sodium iodide.

$$\text{Cl}_2 + 2\text{I}^- \rightarrow 2\text{Cl}^- + \text{I}_2$$

**Observe the lower aqueous layer**

Sodium iodide solution starts colourless. The iodine formed dissolves slightly to give a brown solution, so the lower layer changes from colourless to brown.

**Observe the upper hexane layer**

Hexane is immiscible and less dense, so it floats on top. Iodine is non-polar and very soluble in hexane, where it gives an intense purple or violet colour. So the upper colourless liquid becomes coloured as iodine is extracted into it.

options.A: Correct. Iodine is liberated by displacement, turning the aqueous layer brown, and it then dissolves preferentially in hexane to give a violet coloured upper layer.
options.B: Incorrect. The lower layer does become brown, but the upper layer does not stay unchanged. Iodine is much more soluble in hexane and colours it strongly violet.
options.C: Incorrect. This reverses the starting point. Sodium iodide solution is colourless, not brown. Brown is the colour after iodine is formed, not before.
options.D: Incorrect on both layers. The aqueous layer starts colourless and becomes brown, not the reverse, and the hexane layer picks up iodine and becomes coloured.
